title: Are humans wired to survive?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss whether humans are "wired to survive," tied to a companion article Chuck wrote on How Stuff Works. They cover the case of Mitsutaka Uchikoshi, a Japanese hiker who was unconscious for 24 days and survived with a very low body temperature, possibly a hibernation-like state; the fight-or-flight response as evidence of survival instincts; natural selection illustrated with red and brown worms; newborn crying as an innate survival behavior; a 2005 Arizona State study linking the instinct to recognize living things to modern prejudice; a BBC "Human Instinct" experiment on smelling T-shirts to choose partners with different immune genes; and Richard Dawkins' idea that genes are the driving force behind human behavior. The episode ends with a sponsor read and a brief mention of an economic stimulus rebate article by Jane McGrath.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show with banter about the Braves and set up the question of whether humans are wired to survive. A Visa sponsor read is included.

segments.title: Mitsutaka Uchikoshi and hibernation-like survival
segments.summary: Chuck describes Japanese hiker Mitsutaka Uchikoshi, who was found unconscious after 24 days with a body temperature of about 71 degrees Fahrenheit and nearly no heartbeat. The hosts say he may have entered a hibernation-like state. Chuck comments on his own attempts to lower his body temperature.

segments.title: Fight or flight and natural selection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the fight-or-flight response as involuntary physical evidence of survival wiring. Josh explains the hormonal response and ties it to Darwin's natural selection, using a red and brown worm example.

segments.title: Infant crying and innate survival behaviors
segments.summary: The hosts compare human newborns, who are born defenseless, with animals like horses and sharks. They say a baby's cry is an innate survival signal whose volume and pitch change with urgency.

segments.title: Arizona State study on recognizing living things and prejudice
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 2005 Arizona State study proposing that the instinct to notice living things may relate to modern prejudice. The researchers argued that people in small tribes saw outsiders as threats, and that this relic may explain xenophobia.

segments.title: BBC experiment on smelling T-shirts and immune systems
segments.summary: Josh describes a BBC Human Instinct segment in which six women slept in T-shirts that a host then smelled. He preferred shirts from women whose immune genes differed from his own, which the hosts present as support for mate selection for robust offspring. They note the test is unscientific.

segments.title: Richard Dawkins and genes as survival vehicles
segments.summary: Josh describes zoologist Richard Dawkins' view that humans are vehicles for genes and that our instincts serve to pass genes along. The hosts agree it supports the idea that we are wired to survive. Josh mixes up Dawkins with Richard Dawson, and they note the confusion.

segments.title: Sign-off, Visa read, and stimulus rebate article
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and promote Chuck's article. They then discuss the 2008 economic stimulus rebate checks and mention Jane McGrath's article on whether tax rebates prevent economic downturns. A Visa read and a sign-off close the episode.
